title: Mangalorean Chicken Ghee Roast: The Indulgent Dish Nutritionists Actually Endorse
excerpt: Born in a Kundapur restaurant kitchen in 1957, this fiery coastal Karnataka classic packs 34 grams of protein per serving — and modern science is catching up to what Ayurveda always knew about ghee.
body:
• Chicken ghee roast originated in 1957 at Shetty Lunch Home in Kundapur, Karnataka, and has become one of India's most iconic coastal dishes.
  • Each serving delivers roughly 34 grams of protein and 320-435 calories, with ghee providing fat-soluble vitamins A and E alongside a high smoke point ideal for Indian cooking.
  • A 2024 review in the Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine found 774 references to ghee's therapeutic benefits across 3,000 years of Ayurvedic texts, with modern research validating its role in gut health and nutrient absorption.
  • The recipe uses Byadagi chilies for vibrant color without excessive heat, and all key ingredients are available at most Indian grocery stores worldwide.

Few dishes capture the soul of coastal Karnataka quite like chicken ghee roast. With its deep crimson masala, the fragrance of dry-roasted spices, and the unmistakable richness of clarified butter coating every piece of bone-in chicken, this Mangalorean classic has long straddled the line between guilty pleasure and comfort food. What's changing is the guilt part.

Nutritionists are reassessing ghee's place in a balanced diet, and research suggests that ghee-based dishes like this one fit comfortably into a high-protein, moderate-fat eating plan. At roughly 34 grams of protein and 320-435 calories per serving, chicken ghee roast is more than indulgence — it's a legitimate meal.

From a Kundapur Kitchen to Global Tables

The dish traces its origins to 1957, when Prabhavathi Shetty, working alongside her husband Tejappa at their restaurant Shetty Lunch Home in Kundapur, experimented with their existing chicken sukka recipe. She added generous amounts of ghee and swapped in Byadagi chilies — the mild, deeply pigmented variety native to northern Karnataka — for sharper red chilies. The result was a dish that looked fiery but tasted nuanced: tangy from tamarind, warm from dry-roasted spices, slightly sweet from jaggery, and impossibly rich from ghee.

"The essence of chicken ghee roast lies in its perfect balance — the generous use of ghee, the distinctive Byadgi chilies, and the careful balance of spices create that unmistakable flavor."

— HomeCookingShow.in, on the Shetty Lunch Home legacy

Shetty Lunch Home became a culinary landmark, eventually expanding to Mangalore. The dish inspired prawn, mushroom, and paneer variations, and today it anchors menus at South Indian restaurants from Bengaluru to Birmingham.

Why Nutritionists Are Warming Up to Ghee

For decades, ghee was collateral damage in the war on dietary fat. That narrative has shifted. A comprehensive review published in the Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine examined 4,000 references to milk products across eleven classical Ayurvedic texts spanning 3,000 years. Ghee appeared 774 times — more than any other milk-based product — with benefits grouped into 15 clusters including digestive health, cognitive function, and immune support.

Modern research confirms that ghee's high smoke point (232°C to 252°C) makes it far more stable for high-heat Indian cooking methods like tadka and roasting than many vegetable oils. Bengaluru-based nutritionist Anupama Menon has noted that ghee contains a favorable omega-6 to omega-3 ratio between 2:1 and 4:1, and is a meaningful source of vitamins A and E. "The narrative has changed now and people value ghee as an ingredient for cooking," Menon told Livemint, while cautioning that one to two teaspoons daily remains the general recommendation.

The Recipe: Authentic Mangalorean Chicken Ghee Roast

This version stays true to the Kundapur original. Total time is about 90 minutes, including marination.

Ingredients (serves 4-5):

Marinade: 1 kg bone-in chicken, juice of 1 lemon, 1 tbsp curd, 1 tsp each salt, red chili powder, and turmeric, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste.

Masala paste: 8-10 Byadagi or Kashmiri dried red chilies, 2 tsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp each cumin and fennel seeds, ½ tsp each fenugreek seeds and peppercorns, 4 garlic cloves, 1 tbsp tamarind pulp.

For cooking: 4 tbsp ghee (divided), 3 sprigs curry leaves, 1 tsp grated jaggery, salt to taste.

Method: Marinate chicken for at least one hour. Dry-roast chilies and whole spices on low heat until fragrant, cool, then grind with garlic, tamarind, and water into a smooth paste. Heat 2 tablespoons ghee in a kadai, sear chicken on high heat for 10 minutes, then remove. Cook the masala paste in the same pan for 10 minutes. Add remaining ghee and cook until the ghee separates. Return chicken, add jaggery and salt, cook covered for 15 minutes. Finish with curry leaves. Serve with neer dosa or steamed rice.

Making It Work Abroad

Chicken ghee roast is one of the more accessible South Indian dishes to replicate overseas. Byadagi chilies are stocked at most Indian grocery stores in North America, the UK, the Middle East, and Australia; Kashmiri chilies work as a substitute. Tamarind paste is widely available in mainstream supermarkets. The masala can be prepared in bulk and frozen for up to two weeks, making weeknight cooking faster. A side of cucumber raita offsets the richness.

This dish sits at an intersection of tradition and modern nutrition — one that Indian grandmothers always considered nourishing, and that nutritionists armed with better data on saturated fats are increasingly willing to endorse. The key is balance: use good-quality ghee in moderation, and build the rest of your meal around vegetables and whole grains. As Prabhavathi Shetty understood nearly seven decades ago, the best cooking delivers both flavor and substance.
